title: Convert a `String` date "2020-01-15" to `LocalDate` and calculate the employee's tenure in years.
shortTitle: Convert a String date "2020-01-15" to LocalDate and calculate the employee's tenure in years

s1_definition.profdef: `LocalDate.parse(text)` parses an ISO-8601 date string into a `LocalDate`. `ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(joinDate, LocalDate.now())` or `Period.between(...).getYears()` then computes the completed years of tenure.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya reads a joining date written as text, turns it into a real calendar date, and then counts how many full years the employee has worked since then.
s1_definition.oneliner: `LocalDate.parse("2020-01-15")`, then `ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(join, now)` gives completed tenure years.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `LocalDate.parse(text)` parses an ISO-8601 date string into a `LocalDate`. `ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(joinDate, LocalDate.now())` or `Period.between(...).getYears()` then computes the completed years of tenure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya reads a joining date written as text, turns it into a real calendar date, and then counts how many full years the employee has worked since then.

**One line to remember:** `LocalDate.parse("2020-01-15")`, then `ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(join, now)` gives completed tenure years.

sections.s2_technical:
`LocalDate.parse("2020-01-15")` uses the default ISO date format, so no explicit formatter is needed for yyyy-MM-dd strings. For other formats you pass a `DateTimeFormatter`. The result is an immutable `LocalDate` representing that calendar day with no time or zone.

To compute tenure, `ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(joinDate, LocalDate.now())` returns the number of complete years elapsed as a long, correctly accounting for whether the anniversary has passed this year. `Period.between(join, now).getYears()` gives the years component of a year-month-day breakdown, which is also complete years. Both respect leap years because the date API models the real calendar.

The senior nuance is that LocalDate is zone-free, so "now" depends on the system clock's zone; for correctness I often inject a `Clock` so the calculation is testable and deterministic. I also handle a malformed date string by catching `DateTimeParseException` and treating it as invalid input rather than letting it crash a batch. Using the java.time API instead of the old Date and Calendar avoids a whole class of timezone and mutability bugs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores joining dates as text and must compute each employee's completed years of service for a loyalty benefit.

This is exactly what LocalDate.parse plus ChronoUnit YEARS between does — it turns the text into a date and counts full years of tenure.

The code defines a `TenureService` with an injected clock and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the text "2020-01-15" and a fixed "today" of 2025-06-01.

Step 1: LocalDate.parse reads the ISO text into the date 15 January 2020.

Step 2: LocalDate.now with the fixed clock gives 1 June 2025.

Step 3: ChronoUnit YEARS between counts complete years from Jan 2020 to Jun 2025, which is five because the January anniversary has passed.

Step 4: For the malformed "not-a-date", parse throws DateTimeParseException, caught and returned as the sentinel minus one.

```
INFO: Joined 2020-01-15 → tenure = 5 years
INFO: bad date → -1
```

```

    │ → 2020-01-15
    │ ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(2020-01-15, 2025-06-01)
    ▼
  5 years   (anniversary passed)

  "not-a-date" → DateTimeParseException → catch → -1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To turn a joining date stored as text into a usable date I call LocalDate dot parse, which reads an ISO yyyy-MM-dd string directly without any explicit formatter; for other formats I pass a DateTimeFormatter. The result is an immutable LocalDate with no time or zone attached. To compute tenure I use ChronoUnit dot YEARS dot between of the join date and today, which returns the number of complete years elapsed, correctly accounting for whether the anniversary has already passed this year.

At the National Bank of India this drives a loyalty benefit based on completed years of service. I deliberately inject a Clock so that "now" is not tied to the live system clock, which makes the calculation deterministic and unit-testable, and I catch DateTimeParseException so a malformed date string is treated as invalid input rather than crashing the whole batch.

The senior point I stress is to use the java dot time API rather than the old Date and Calendar classes, because java dot time is immutable, thread-safe, and models the real calendar including leap years, which eliminates a whole category of timezone and mutability bugs. The combination of LocalDate for a zone-free calendar day and ChronoUnit for precise differences is exactly the right tool for a tenure calculation.
